video_title: Anthropic’s IPO in Question,  Midterms Hit AI, Nasdaq Drops 5%, and RSI Accelerates | #309
gist: After a Democratic midterm sweep in which opposition to big tech and data centers became a major issue (Goldman: 45% of planned US data center buildout could face restrictions), the Nasdaq fell 5.5% and Nvidia 9.3%, and the hosts debate whether Anthropic's IPO gets pushed. Their core view is that the backlash is a cyclical blip: it pushes compute to friendly states, Canada and orbit, and software-only recursive self-improvement (METR finds Anthropic's AI progress running about 1.9x its historical rate) keeps progress going anyway. The real long-term risks they name are compute scarcity locked up by a handful of buyers and a government 'safety cartel' controlling who gets compute.

insights.claim: A co-host argues Anthropic is unlikely to delay its IPO over the midterm results, because Polymarket odds already clearly signaled the outcome three to four weeks earlier, when Anthropic chose to launch its roadshow.
insights.speaker: co-host
insights.so_what: The IPO probably proceeds on schedule; any adjustment shows up in price, not timing.
insights.quote: the polyarket odds were really really clear, you know, three four weeks ago and that's when they pulled the trigger on the road show

insights.claim: Alex Wissner-Gross notes public reporting that investment bankers are pushing Anthropic's IPO valuation down, while Anthropic may want liquidity quickly ahead of a tougher regulatory and statutory environment expected in January.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Expect pressure for a lower IPO price with a fast timeline, as Anthropic tries to list before new rules arrive.
insights.quote: there there's lots of public reporting now that investment bankers are trying to force down the IPO valuation

insights.claim: Dave Blundin compares the Anthropic IPO to Meta's: Wall Street could not absorb that much supply, forced a markdown, the stock traded down, and buying a few weeks after the IPO turned out to be one of the best trades ever, with Meta now up roughly 20-30x.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Weak trading right after a mega-IPO can be a buying opportunity rather than a sign the company is failing.
insights.quote: it was the best buy in the history of the world if you just waited out a few weeks after the IPO and all the doom and gloom and catastrophe

insights.claim: Alex Wissner-Gross argues that the Anthropic and OpenAI IPOs face a headwind from local and national regulation and legislation, much as fears that mobile would cannibalize its web business hung over Facebook's IPO, and that Meta came through that.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: He treats regulatory risk as a temporary story at IPO time, not a permanent problem for the business.
insights.quote: The headwind for anthropic and open AI IPOs is the regulatory and statutory and legislative environment both at the local level and the national level.

insights.claim: Anthropic is described as approaching a revenue run rate of about $100 billion a year, which the host calls extraordinary given how quickly it got there.
insights.speaker: Salim Ismail (host)
insights.so_what: The revenue scale behind Anthropic's IPO valuation.
insights.quote: a company generating close to a revenue run rate of 100 billion a year in such a short time

insights.claim: Alex Wissner-Gross estimates from public sources that Anthropic's total compute footprint will be about 4 GW by the end of 2026 and could reach 16-18 GW in 2027-2028.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: A roughly 4x compute ramp means sustained, very large demand for power and chips.
insights.quote: Anthropic's total compute footprint by the end of this year at call it 4 gawattish

insights.claim: In the 2026 midterms, which Democrats swept, polls showed 56% opposition to big tech and data centers. Goldman Sachs estimates 45% of planned US data center buildout could face restrictions, and candidates calling for pauses won or led in 12 governor races.
insights.speaker: Salim Ismail (host)
insights.so_what: Regulatory risk now has a number attached: nearly half the planned US AI buildout is in play.
insights.quote: Goldman Sachs estimates 45% of planned US center buildout could be face restrictions

insights.claim: The host argues that political and community resistance may become a bigger constraint on AI infrastructure than chips or capital.
insights.speaker: Salim Ismail (host)
insights.so_what: Permitting and local politics become key variables for AI infrastructure investment.
insights.quote: political and community resistance may actually become the biggest constraint on AI infrastructure more so than even chips or capital

insights.claim: Dave Blundin argues that data center buildout will move state by state toward welcoming jurisdictions. Texas is the big loss given how much construction is there, while Tennessee (where Elon Musk put xAI's Colossus) and Virginia benefit.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Where data centers are located matters more now; states that welcome them gain GDP.
insights.quote: Put all of Colossus in Tennessee, not in Texas.

insights.claim: Dave Blundin calls it unprecedented that a major technology like AI is a dominant election issue, and that a party historically backed by Meta and Google is attacking tech and Dario Amodei, even though these same companies now own the media channels.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: AI labs have about two years before the next election to work out a political strategy.
insights.quote: Now, all media happens to be owned by these exact same companies that have developed AI.

insights.claim: Alex Wissner-Gross suggests a 'grand bargain': instead of banning data centers, states and municipalities with energy and powered land should use their temporary leverage to demand hyperscaler-funded benefits such as free school lunches, county medical care or tax rebates for residents, before compute moves to orbit.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Expect community benefit agreements to become a standard cost of building data centers on Earth.
insights.quote: There is a trade. There is a grand bargain to be struck.

insights.claim: Alex Wissner-Gross says consumers still lack a killer app for reasoning models (OpenAI shifted its reasoning focus from consumers to enterprises), and that frontier labs could win the public back by solving the top 5,000 diseases in silico within one to two years and marketing it heavily.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Labs' public standing, and their freedom to build, may depend on visible wins like curing diseases.
insights.quote: Use super intelligence. Solve the top 5,000 diseases. Market the heck out of it to the general public

insights.claim: Dave Blundin pushes back that disease cures take longer than an election cycle because of the FDA. A beloved consumer AI product, such as a Jony Ive device or personal agent that visibly gets throttled without data centers, would move voters more, because pausing data centers does not cut off drugs people already have, like GLP-1s.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: A consumer AI hardware or agent product could be the political turning point before the next election.
insights.quote: pausing the data center doesn't stop the supply

insights.claim: The industry responded to the backlash without slowing down: SpaceX is building about 3.6 GW on Earth with a target of 13 GW by the end of next year, OpenAI announced a community compact to cover energy costs and its CFO said infrastructure spending will not slow, Google announced a $17 billion Wyoming data center, and Meta warned of construction challenges.
insights.speaker: Salim Ismail (host)
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler capex plans are holding up despite political pressure.
insights.quote: Google's announced a $17 billion Wyoming data center

insights.claim: Dave Blundin says the backlash speeds up work on more efficient algorithms and power-efficient hardware (already visible in his deal flow) and pushes data centers toward Canada, which has the best power supply per capita in North America. A Canadian project started now would come online in about 18 months, around the next election.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Canadian power and data center projects, and AI efficiency startups, become more attractive.
insights.quote: the power supply is overwhelmingly better per capita in Canada than it is anywhere else in in North America

insights.claim: Dave Blundin urged European energy CEOs to build every form of power generation they can because all of it will be used, and found they had not been considering it, being absorbed in local issues such as replacing Russian gas with LNG.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Europe is missing an opportunity to supply AI power; Spain's decision to keep nuclear running longer is a small positive sign.
insights.quote: go build every power generation you possibly can. it's all going to be used

insights.claim: The host argues that the singularity is now limited less by technology than by political, financial and social institutions that improve slower than linearly, and that society will react more and more sharply as AI accelerates.
insights.speaker: Salim Ismail (host)
insights.so_what: Expect continued backlash; how fast institutions adapt is the key variable.
insights.quote: our political, our financial, our social institutions are sublinear

insights.claim: After the midterms, the Nasdaq fell 5.5%, the S&P 500 more than 4%, big semiconductor stocks 12%, Nvidia 9.3% and Korea's market 6%, as investors reassessed infrastructure spending and regulatory uncertainty.
insights.speaker: Salim Ismail (host)
insights.so_what: The market is putting a political discount on the AI infrastructure trade.
insights.quote: NASDAQ was down 5.5%. The SNP dropped more than 4%. Big semiconductor stocks 12%, Nvidia 9.3%. Korea dropped 6%.

insights.claim: Dave Blundin says Nvidia and the hyperscalers had been sliding for four to five weeks before the election, jumped briefly, then fell. The market is pricing in slower power and AI construction for projects that are planned but not yet zoned, not a halt to approved construction, along with a better chance for China to catch up.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: The risk sits in future projects that have not been permitted; projects already approved, with large sunk costs, are mostly safe.
insights.quote: I don't think there's much expectation that existing construction on on approved projects is going to stop.

insights.claim: Dave Blundin expects the short-term effect to be more expensive AI and fewer breakthroughs, citing Elon Musk's warning that about 15 GW of compute could sit idle because it cannot find a liquid-cooled data center to plug into.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: The bottleneck shifts from chips to powered, cooled data center space, which helps owners of ready data center capacity.
insights.quote: there's going to be about 15 gawatts of idle compute capability that can't find a data center with liquid cooling to plug into

insights.claim: Alex Wissner-Gross argues that if politics restricts compute supply while demand keeps soaring, compute prices will rise. He sees that as a healthy signal that will steer capital to offshore, underwater, underground and orbital data centers.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Rising compute prices would benefit existing compute owners and alternative data center locations.
insights.quote: One would expect the price of compute to go up.

insights.claim: Alex Wissner-Gross argues that halting all new US data center construction would probably crash public equities but would barely slow AI progress, perhaps costing a few months against China, because software-only recursive self-improvement is now enough to keep advancing.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: He separates AI progress from AI infrastructure equity returns; the stocks carry the political risk, not the technology.
insights.quote: presumably public equities would collapse if all new construction on data centers were halted

insights.claim: Dave Blundin says frontier labs report that every chip is in use and token demand is insatiable, citing Anthropic's S-1 growth figures, so the constraint is building chips and data centers, not demand.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: AI demand looks safe; supply is where the risk is.
insights.quote: every chip is getting used and the demand for the tokens is insane

insights.claim: An independent 11-week METR study found Anthropic's AI development accelerating at about 1.9x its historical rate, with roughly 80% of the speed-up attributed to AI assisting AI research and no bottleneck seen for at least the next year.
insights.speaker: Salim Ismail (host)
insights.so_what: First measured evidence that AI is speeding up its own development.
insights.quote: anthropics AI development is accelerating at approximately 1.9 times its historical rate

insights.claim: Alex Wissner-Gross notes that progress is within 10-15% of where the AI 2027 scenario predicted for November 2026, and that a model code-named 'model 4' on METR's charts sits above the exponential trend line.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Fast-takeoff timelines are tracking reality closely.
insights.quote: Look at model 4 on that chart.

insights.claim: Dave Blundin cites Anthropic's internal token use for development rising 235x in six months, plus METR data showing a large shift of compute from external products to internal work, as proof that recursive self-improvement is underway.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Labs are using more of their own compute internally, which limits external capacity and signals self-improvement.
insights.quote: the use of tokens for internal development and anthropic is up 235x in the last 6 months

insights.claim: Dave Blundin warns that the public is getting less inside information on AI progress: Dario Amodei, once the industry's candid voice, is in an IPO quiet period, labs have gone quiet after criticism from Washington, and the remaining coverage is driven by ad views and panic.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Mainstream coverage may understate how fast progress is moving; read it skeptically.
insights.quote: Now he's in a quiet period going into an IPO.

insights.claim: Alex Wissner-Gross defines recursive self-improvement as the point where each additional unit of compute is more likely to go to an AI researcher than a human one, and says Anthropic's charts show we are already past 50% on that measure.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: A concrete way to measure RSI: the share of research compute going to AI researchers.
insights.quote: I think we're already to the right of 50% of compute on margin being devoted to AI researchers.

insights.claim: Dave Blundin argues that AI only needs a few good research ideas to beat a top human like Noam Brown. Even if the AI has 1 good idea in 10 versus Noam's 6, it can generate unlimited ideas and test them all in code, which is why labs keep pulling compute inside.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: AI research is a numbers game; volume of ideas beats hit rate.
insights.quote: As long as you're hitting balls over the wall, you have an infinite number of pitches and you just test them all.

insights.claim: Alex Wissner-Gross notes that solving Navier-Stokes reportedly took about 10,000 agents, while the later 'slop drop' took about three agent-hours per solved problem. He says new models now have learnable AI research taste that post-training can raise from 1-in-10 to 9-in-10 good ideas.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: The cost of solving hard research problems is collapsing.
insights.quote: it was three agent hours per solved problem

insights.claim: Alex Wissner-Gross predicts that by around early 2027, frontier models will move to continuous release instead of discrete launches, much as Google switched from announcing search index expansions to updating the index in real time.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Named model launches will matter less as a competitive event.
insights.quote: at some point it's just going to be continuous release and I I would expect that to happen early 2027 or so

insights.claim: Alex Wissner-Gross says the biggest architecture change of the past two months has been a shift from conventional transformers to looped transformers, likely found through neural architecture search. He predicts, as a falsifiable claim, that the end-state architecture will be interpretable and even beautiful, not alien.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: He plays down the risk that self-improving AI becomes uninterpretable.
insights.quote: a transition from conventional transformers

insights.claim: Dave Blundin expects that under hard takeoff, labs will keep more compute internal and move from selling compute to selling what it produces, such as AI-discovered drugs and physical devices.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Frontier labs may become direct competitors in pharma and hardware, not just API vendors.
insights.quote: instead of selling um selling the compute to the world they're selling the product of the compute to the world

insights.claim: Alex Wissner-Gross argues that the 2-3x yearly GDP growth Elon Musk describes will come from bulk-solving grand challenges in science, engineering and medicine, not from infrastructure capex, which is only the opening act. He expects both OpenAI's 'slop drop' style and Anthropic's partnership style of bringing discoveries out.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Long-term value moves from builders of AI infrastructure to whoever applies AI to science and industry.
insights.quote: capex for infrastructure is just the opening act to lay the foundation for what comes next

insights.claim: Alex Wissner-Gross predicts that within a few years, which he calls a conservative outer bound, humanity will be able to send relativistic von Neumann probes in every direction, forcing the Fermi paradox question.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: A long-range speculative implication of RSI.
insights.quote: I think we're within a few years of having the capability of sending relativistic vanoyman probes in every direction

insights.claim: A new 'joules to GDP' paper tested 220 professional tasks across 44 occupations. GLM 5.2 produced the most value, about $70 per task, while the smaller Gemma 4 31B model delivered 2.5x more economic value per joule.
insights.speaker: Salim Ismail (host)
insights.so_what: Small models can win on value per unit of energy, which matters when power is scarce.
insights.quote: the smaller Gemma 4 31 billion model delivered 2.5 times more economic value per jewel

insights.claim: Alex Wissner-Gross observes that Chinese open-weight models beat American open-weight models on economic productivity per watt, probably because they were trained under compute constraints, and he welcomes the pressure on US labs to become more efficient.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Export controls are making Chinese models more efficient.
insights.quote: the Chinese openweight models are beating the American openweight models in terms of economic productivity per watt

insights.claim: Alex Wissner-Gross argues that watts or joules may be the wrong long-term denominator, preferring dollars in versus dollars out, because reversible computing or quantum dissipationless AI could make the Landauer limit effectively obsolete.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Energy-efficiency benchmarks could become meaningless if energy-free (reversible) computing arrives.
insights.quote: reversible computing could make the land hour limit effectively obsolete

insights.claim: Dave Blundin describes a race between small task-specific models and frontier models. Startups can build a 50B-parameter specialist model for about $20 million instead of a multi-trillion-parameter model, and customers prefer $300,000 token experiments to $10 million ones, but frontier models keep improving and wiping out those gains.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Specialist small-model startups are a live investment theme with an unclear winner.
insights.quote: nobody nobody wants to burn $10 million of tokens and then realize they've got nothing to show for it

insights.claim: As a provocation, the host calculates that an AI cluster earns about $8 billion of revenue per GW (Anthropic at about $100B with a couple of GW), while New York City produces about $1.2 trillion of GDP on 5.5 GW, roughly $200B per GW, making a human city about 30x more energy-efficient at creating value.
insights.speaker: Salim Ismail (host)
insights.so_what: He offers it as a benchmark to track as AI output scales, while admitting it compares unlike things.
insights.quote: an AI cluster roughly yields about 8 billion in revenue per gawatt

insights.claim: Dave Blundin rebuts that the city comparison ignores human 'training' costs and that Anthropic's revenue undercounts the value created: his office used half a billion tokens in one day, about the work of 5,000 brilliant workers, for roughly $5,000, or about $1 per worker per day.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: AI customers capture far more value than labs collect in revenue, which suggests prices have room to rise.
insights.quote: And it cost about $5,000. So about a buck per worker per day.

insights.claim: Dave Blundin warns that Google, Anthropic and xAI have reserved nearly all US compute and chips, including effectively all TSMC capacity, for years. He calls for a 'right to compute' and compares the situation to the Rockefeller era, with the DOJ largely inactive.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Compute access could become an antitrust and election issue; startups risk being starved of compute.
insights.quote: if you want a thriving entrepreneurial America you have to have some kind of a right to compute

insights.claim: Dave Blundin says his NVIDIA NVL72 GB300 machine comes online February 1 only because of an inside contact, a pilot client was turned away by a cloud for being too small, some neoclouds are having a rough month, and Modal is growing fast and buying up all the capacity it can find.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: GPU scarcity is hitting smaller buyers hard and will likely last three to seven years.
insights.quote: Right. This is going to be like three to five years, seven years of this.

insights.claim: Dave Blundin argues that losing access to AI would be like losing every form of power. Even a bakery without AI would face a 30-50% operating margin disadvantage against a neighbor that has it.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Access to AI is becoming a basic competitive requirement for every business.
insights.quote: will operate with at least a 30 40 50% operating margin advantage

insights.claim: The White House issued NSTM-6, a national policy on synthetic DNA and RNA screening in response to AI-enabled biological risks. It requires federally funded researchers to use approved synthesis providers, screen sequences of generally 50 or more nucleotides, verify customers and keep records for eight years.
insights.speaker: Salim Ismail (host)
insights.so_what: Regulators are targeting physical chokepoints where AI meets the real world, which favors approved DNA synthesis vendors.
insights.quote: screening generally covering sequences of 50 or more nucleotides

insights.claim: Alex Wissner-Gross supports regulating physical actions like DNA synthesis, citing Treasury's anti-counterfeiting yellow-dot precedent with printers. He says the real nightmare is a 'safety cartel' that limits compute and superintelligent thought to government-approved vendors, or GPUs regulated like uranium under the NRC.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Rules on actions are tolerable; licensing of compute would be the worst-case regulatory capture.
insights.quote: We have a legal we have a legal tradition in the west of regulating actions and not thoughts.

insights.claim: Alex Wissner-Gross predicts that the DNA synthesis approach will extend to general-purpose robots, with licensed manufacturers and black-box recording and retention of every actuation command.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Humanoid robot makers may face licensing and data retention compliance.
insights.quote: If we're seeing it with biological sequence synthesis, probably see it with robotics as well.

themes.theme: Orbital compute and the Dyson swarm

insights.claim: Alex Wissner-Gross argues that the terrestrial backlash is the biggest boost possible over the next year or two for orbital data centers, because the Outer Space Treaty and Artemis Accords regulate more lightly and are less exposed to two-year election cycles.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Political risk on Earth strengthens the investment case for space-based compute.
insights.quote: I I do think this is the greatest shot in the arm for building out the Dyson swarm that we could have seen on the time scale of a year or two.

insights.claim: Dave Blundin counters that in the best case, orbital compute is only a couple percent of all compute in two years before growing exponentially, while ASI arrives within that two-year window, so terrestrial constraints still matter.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin
insights.so_what: Orbital compute does not rescue near-term AI capacity.
insights.quote: best case that's a couple percent of all compute in two years and then it's on an exponential

insights.claim: New Zealand photographer Brendan Larson combined 578 photographs over two hours above Mount Taranaki, capturing nearly 15,000 satellite trails from about 1,400 satellites, which the hosts treat as an early image of a Dyson swarm.
insights.speaker: Salim Ismail (host)
insights.so_what: Low Earth orbit is becoming dense infrastructure, raising questions about ownership and congestion.
insights.quote: capturing almost 15,000 satellite trail appearances from about 1,400 satellites

insights.claim: Alex Wissner-Gross, disclosing a financial interest in Lonestar, says Starlink, Elon Musk's planned AI satellites, StarCloud and other neo space clouds amount to a baby Dyson swarm. He argues sun-synchronous orbit has room for a lot of compute with less Kessler-syndrome risk, and expects a visible SSO 'halo' of compute.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: Sun-synchronous orbit compute operators are the main space beneficiaries of the theme.
insights.quote: SSO is pretty roomy. Uh so less concerned about Kesler syndrome.

insights.claim: Alex Wissner-Gross closes by calling the political swing a cyclical blip on a secular superintelligence trend, citing Ray Kurzweil's observation that world wars and depressions have had almost no effect on the price of compute.
insights.speaker: Alex Wissner-Gross
insights.so_what: He reads political selloffs as noise against the long-term compute trend.
insights.quote: world wars, depressions have approximately no impact on the the price of compute
